questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: System and surroundings
questions.question: Which of the following is the standard example of an isolated system?
options: Hot tea kept in an ideal thermos flask
Reactants kept in an open beaker
A reaction mixture in a sealed metal vessel
Water boiling in an open pan

solution.key_concept: An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings.
steps: An ideal thermos flask stops both heat flow and the escape of matter.
Reactants in an open beaker and water in an open pan exchange both matter and energy, so they are open systems.
A sealed metal vessel exchanges energy but not matter, so it is a closed system.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Hot tea kept in an ideal thermos flask
solution.why_not_others: Options 2 and 4 are open systems. Option 3 is a closed system, because heat can pass through the metal walls.
solution.common_trap: Taking any sealed container as isolated. Sealing stops matter exchange but not energy exchange.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: System and surroundings
questions.question: Hot coffee is kept in a tightly sealed steel container on a table, and it slowly cools down. How is the coffee (taken as the system) correctly classified?
options: Closed, because only energy crosses the boundary
Isolated, because the container is sealed
Open, because heat flows to the surroundings
Isolated, because the total energy of the coffee stays constant

solution.key_concept: A closed system exchanges energy but not matter with its surroundings.
steps: The seal prevents any matter from crossing the boundary.
The coffee cools, so heat (energy) leaves through the steel walls.
Energy exchange without matter exchange defines a closed system.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Closed, because only energy crosses the boundary
solution.why_not_others: An isolated system cannot lose heat, and here the energy of the coffee falls. An open system must exchange matter as well, and heat flow alone does not make a system open.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that a sealed container must be isolated.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: System and surroundings
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A reaction mixture kept in a sealed metal vessel is an isolated system.
statements.R: A closed system exchanges energy but not matter with its surroundings.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Classification of systems by what crosses the boundary.
steps: A sealed metal vessel lets heat pass through its walls but keeps matter inside.
Such a vessel is therefore a closed system, not an isolated one, so A is false.
R gives the correct definition of a closed system, so R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options 1, 2 and 3 cannot be correct.
solution.common_trap: Equating 'sealed' with 'isolated'.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: System and surroundings
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Reactants kept in an open beaker form a closed system, because the walls of the beaker prevent any loss of matter.
statements.II: System plus surroundings make up the universe, and the boundary between them may be real or imaginary, rigid or movable.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Open systems exchange matter and energy, and the boundary can be of any kind.
steps: An open beaker allows both matter (for example vapour or gas) and energy to cross, so it is an open system. Statement I is incorrect.
Universe = system + surroundings, and the boundary may be real or imaginary, rigid or movable. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I is false, which rules out options 1 and 3. Statement II is true, which rules out option 2.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that the side walls of a container are enough to stop matter exchange, even though its top is open.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Extensive and intensive properties
questions.question: Which of the following is an intensive property?

solution.key_concept: An intensive property does not depend on the amount of matter present.
steps: If the system is halved, its temperature stays the same in each half.
Volume, enthalpy and mass are each shared between the two halves, so they are extensive.
solution.why_not_others: Volume, enthalpy and mass all depend on the amount of matter.
solution.common_trap: Treating enthalpy as intensive. It is molar enthalpy that is intensive.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Extensive and intensive properties
questions.question: Which of the following sets contains only extensive properties?
options: Heat capacity, molar heat capacity, enthalpy

solution.key_concept: U, H, S, G, C, m, V and n are extensive. Ratios such as density and molar quantities are intensive.
steps: Density is a ratio of two extensive properties, so it is intensive.
Temperature is intensive.
Molar heat capacity, $C_m = C/n$, is intensive.
Gibbs energy, entropy and heat capacity are all extensive.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Gibbs energy, entropy, heat capacity
solution.why_not_others: Each of the other sets contains one intensive property: density, temperature or molar heat capacity.
solution.common_trap: Confusing heat capacity (extensive) with molar heat capacity (intensive).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Extensive and intensive properties
questions.question: A homogeneous sample has density $\rho$, heat capacity $C$ and temperature $T$. It is divided into two identical halves. What are the corresponding values for each half?

solution.key_concept: Extensive properties are shared between the halves, while intensive properties stay unchanged.
steps: Heat capacity is extensive, so each half has $C/2$.
Density is (m/2)/(V/2) = $\rho$, so it is intensive and unchanged.
Temperature is intensive and stays $T$.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 halves the intensive properties. Option 2 fails to halve the extensive heat capacity. Option 4 wrongly halves the density.
solution.common_trap: Halving the density because the mass is halved, and forgetting that the volume is halved too.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Extensive and intensive properties
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Volume divided by number of moles

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Extensive; shared between the two halves of a divided system

list_II.label: IV
list_II.text: Heat capacity divided by number of moles

solution.key_concept: The ratio of two extensive properties is intensive.
steps: Density = m/V, so A-III.
$C_m = C/n$, so B-IV.
Molar volume = V/n, so C-I.
Heat capacity C is extensive, so D-II.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 swaps $C$ and $C_m$. Option 2 swaps density and molar volume. Option 4 is mismatched throughout.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that molar heat capacity is extensive.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Extensive and intensive properties
questions.question: Which of the following statements about extensive and intensive properties are correct?

statements.A: The ratio of two extensive properties is always an intensive property.
statements.B: Specific heat is intensive, whereas heat capacity is extensive.
statements.C: Standard electrode potential $E^\circ$ is extensive because it depends on the amount of substance reacting.
statements.D: Extensive properties are additive, whereas intensive properties are not.
statements.E: Surface tension and viscosity are extensive properties.

options: A, B, C and D only

solution.key_concept: Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of matter. Extensive properties do, and they are additive.
steps: A is true. Examples are density = m/V and molar volume = V/n.
B is true. Specific heat c is intensive, while C is extensive.
C is false because $E^\circ$ is intensive.
D is true.
E is false because surface tension and viscosity are intensive.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and D only
solution.why_not_others: Options 2 and 4 include statement C, and option 3 includes statement E. Both of these statements are false.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that $E^\circ$ doubles when the reaction is doubled. It is an intensive property.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: State functions and types of processes
questions.question: Which of the following is a path function?

solution.key_concept: Path functions depend on how a change is carried out, while state functions depend only on the initial and final states.
steps: H, S and G are state functions.
Work w depends on the path followed.
solution.why_not_others: Enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy are all state functions.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that every energy-related quantity is a state function.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: State functions and types of processes
questions.question: A system undergoes a complete cyclic process. Which of the following quantities is NOT necessarily zero for the cycle?

solution.key_concept: Over a complete cycle, the change in every state function is zero, but q and w need not be zero.
steps: U, H and G are state functions, so their changes over the cycle are zero.
q is a path function, so its value over the cycle can be non-zero.
solution.why_not_others: $\Delta U$, $\Delta H$ and $\Delta G$ are each zero for any cycle.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that q = 0 for a cycle simply because $\Delta U = 0$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: State functions and types of processes
questions.question: A gas changes from state X to state Y along path 1, absorbing 50 J of heat while 20 J of work is done by the gas. Along a different path 2 between the same two states, the gas absorbs 40 J of heat. What is the work $w$ for path 2 (sign convention: work done on the system is positive)?

solution.key_concept: q + w = $\Delta U$ is a state function, so it has the same value for both paths.
steps: Path 1: $q = +50$ J and $w = -20$ J, so $\Delta U = +30$ J.
Path 2: $\Delta U$ is again $+30$ J.
solution.why_not_others: +10 J has the wrong sign. -20 J assumes work is the same on both paths, but work is a path function. +30 J is the value of $\Delta U$, not w.
solution.common_trap: Treating w as a state function.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: State functions and types of processes
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: For an ideal gas undergoing an isothermal process, $\Delta U = 0$.
statements.R: In an isothermal process, no heat is exchanged between the system and the surroundings.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Isothermal means constant T. Adiabatic means q = 0.
steps: At constant T, the internal energy of an ideal gas does not change, so $\Delta U = 0$ and A is true.
q = 0 defines an adiabatic process. In an isothermal process heat is exchanged (q = -w), so R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R is false, so options 1, 2 and 4 cannot be correct.
solution.common_trap: Confusing isothermal with adiabatic.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: State functions and types of processes
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Over a complete cycle, the entropy change of the system is zero, even though q and w for the cycle may be non-zero.
statements.II: Since q and w are path functions, their sum q + w also depends on the path followed.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: State functions return to their initial values over a cycle. The sum q + w equals $\Delta U$, which is a state function.
steps: S is a state function, so $\Delta S$ = 0 over a cycle, while q and w can be non-zero. Statement I is correct.
q + w = $\Delta U$, which does not depend on the path. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II is false, which rules out options 1 and 4. Statement I is true, which rules out option 2.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that the sum of two path functions must also be a path function.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: First law: work, heat, internal energy and enthalpy
questions.question: A gas absorbs 300 J of heat and does 120 J of work on the surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?

solution.key_concept: First law: $\Delta U = q + w$.
steps: Heat is absorbed, so $q = +300$ J.
Work is done by the gas, so $w = -120$ J.
solution.why_not_others: +420 J takes w as positive. -180 J and -420 J reverse the signs.
solution.common_trap: Taking work done by the system as positive.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: First law: work, heat, internal energy and enthalpy
questions.question: An ideal gas expands irreversibly from 5 L to 15 L against a constant external pressure of 2 atm. What is the work done (1 L atm = 101.3 J)?

solution.why_not_others: +2026 J has the wrong sign. -20 J leaves L atm unconverted. -1013 J uses 1 atm instead of 2 atm.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting the conversion from L atm to J.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: First law: work, heat, internal energy and enthalpy
questions.question: For the reaction $C_2H_5OH(l) + 3O_2(g) \rightarrow 2CO_2(g) + 3H_2O(l)$ at 298 K, $\Delta U = -1364.0$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. What is $\Delta H$? ($R = 8.314$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)

solution.key_concept: $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$, counting only gaseous moles.
steps: $\Delta n_g = 2 - 3 = -1$, since ethanol and water are liquids.
solution.why_not_others: -1361.5 uses $\Delta n_g = +1$. -1359.0 counts water as a gas ($\Delta n_g = +2$). -1364.0 wrongly assumes $\Delta H = \Delta U$.
solution.common_trap: Counting liquid water in $\Delta n_g$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: First law: work, heat, internal energy and enthalpy
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Free expansion of an ideal gas

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Heating a gas in a rigid closed vessel

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: $q = 0$ and $\Delta U = w \neq 0$; the gas cools

solution.key_concept: First-law results for standard processes.
steps: Free expansion: w = 0, q = 0, $\Delta U$ = 0 and $\Delta T$ = 0, so A-IV.
Isothermal ideal gas: $\Delta U = 0$ and q = -w, so B-III.
Adiabatic: q = 0 and $\Delta U = w$, and the expanding gas cools, so C-I.
Constant volume: w = 0 and $\Delta U = q_V$, so D-II.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 swaps A and B. Option 2 swaps B and C. Option 3 swaps A and C.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that free expansion involves heat absorption, or that adiabatic expansion keeps T constant.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: First law: work, heat, internal energy and enthalpy
questions.question: Which of the following statements are correct?

statements.A: For the same initial and final volumes, the magnitude of reversible isothermal work exceeds that of irreversible work for the expansion of an ideal gas.
statements.B: The enthalpy change of a system equals the heat exchanged at constant volume.
statements.C: For a reaction involving only solids and liquids, $\Delta H = \Delta U$.
statements.D: In an adiabatic expansion, the temperature of an ideal gas rises because the gas does work.
statements.E: When 2 mol of an ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at 300 K from 1 L to 10 L, it absorbs about 11.5 kJ of heat ($R = 8.314$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$).

solution.key_concept: First law: $\Delta H = q_p$, $\Delta U = q_V$, and reversible isothermal work.
steps: A is true. Reversible work is the maximum work obtainable in expansion.
B is false. $\Delta H = q_p$, while $\Delta U = q_V$.
C is true, because $\Delta n_g = 0$.
D is false. In adiabatic expansion $\Delta U = w < 0$, so the gas cools.
E is true. $q = -w = 2.303 \times 2 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times \log 10 = 11488$ J, which is about 11.5 kJ.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 includes statement B. Options 3 and 4 include statement D. Both B and D are false.
solution.common_trap: Confusing $q_p$ with $q_V$, and thinking that adiabatic expansion heats the gas.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Heat capacity and molar heat capacity
questions.question: How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 50 g of water by 10 K? (Specific heat of water = 4.18 J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$)

solution.key_concept: Heat absorbed for a temperature change: $q = mc\Delta T$.
steps: $q = mc\Delta T = 50 \times 4.18 \times 10$
solution.why_not_others: 209 J leaves out $\Delta T$. 41.8 J leaves out the mass. 20.9 kJ comes from a decimal or unit conversion slip.
solution.common_trap: Leaving out one of the three factors (m, c, $\Delta T$), or misconverting J to kJ.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Heat capacity and molar heat capacity
questions.question: 2 mol of a monoatomic ideal gas is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 350 K. What is the heat absorbed by the gas? (R = 8.314 J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)

solution.key_concept: At constant pressure, $q = \Delta H = nC_p\Delta T$. For a monoatomic gas, $C_p = \frac{5}{2}R$.
steps: $\Delta T = 50$ K
$q_p = 2 \times \frac{5}{2} \times 8.314 \times 50$
solution.why_not_others: 1.25 kJ uses $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$. 2.91 kJ uses the diatomic value $C_p = \frac{7}{2}R$. 0.83 kJ is only the expansion work $nR\Delta T$.
solution.common_trap: Using $C_V$ even though the heating is at constant pressure.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Heat capacity and molar heat capacity
questions.question: 3 mol of a diatomic ideal gas is heated at constant pressure so that its temperature rises by 20 K. What is the change in internal energy of the gas?

solution.key_concept: For an ideal gas, $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ for any process. For a diatomic gas, $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$.
steps: The relation $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ holds even at constant pressure.
$\Delta U = 3 \times \frac{5}{2}R \times 20$
$\Delta U = 150R$
solution.why_not_others: $210R$ is $\Delta H$ (it uses $C_p$). $60R$ is $nR\Delta T$, the magnitude of the expansion work. $90R$ uses the monoatomic value of $C_V$.
solution.common_trap: Using $C_p$ for $\Delta U$ because the process is at constant pressure.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Heat capacity and molar heat capacity
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A coffee-cup calorimeter measures $\Delta H$ of a reaction, while a bomb calorimeter measures $\Delta U$.
statements.R: For one mole of an ideal gas, $C_p$ exceeds $C_V$ by R.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: What a calorimeter measures depends on its working condition: constant p gives $q_p = \Delta H$, and constant V gives $q_V = \Delta U$.
steps: A coffee-cup calorimeter works at constant pressure, so it measures $\Delta H$.
A bomb calorimeter works at constant volume, so it measures $\Delta U$. A is therefore true.
The Mayer relation $C_p - C_V = R$ is true, so R is true.
R describes heat capacities of an ideal gas. It does not explain why each calorimeter measures $\Delta H$ or $\Delta U$.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are correct, which rules out options (3) and (4). R does not account for A, which rules out option (1).
solution.common_trap: Linking 'p versus V' in A with '$C_p$ versus $C_V$' in R and assuming R explains A.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Heat capacity and molar heat capacity
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: For an ideal gas, the relation $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ is valid only when the gas is heated at constant volume.
statements.II: When 1 mol of a diatomic ideal gas is heated at constant pressure through 10 K, the heat absorbed is $35R$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ holds for any process of an ideal gas. At constant pressure, $q = nC_p\Delta T$.
steps: U of an ideal gas depends only on T, so $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ for every process. Statement I is false.
For a diatomic gas, $C_p = \frac{7}{2}R$.
$q_p = 1 \times \frac{7}{2}R \times 10 = 35R$. Statement II is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I restricts a general result to constant volume, so it is wrong. Statement II is correct arithmetic.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ needs constant volume because $C_V$ appears in it.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Hess's law of constant heat summation
questions.question: Given: $C(graphite) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)$; $\Delta H = -393.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ and $CO(g) + \frac{1}{2}O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)$; $\Delta H = -283.0$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. What is the standard enthalpy of formation of $CO(g)$?

solution.key_concept: By Hess's law, $\Delta_f H(CO) = \Delta_c H(C) - \Delta_c H(CO)$.
steps: Write the first equation as given.
Reverse the second equation: $CO_2 \rightarrow CO + \frac{1}{2}O_2$; $\Delta H = +283.0$ kJ.
Add the two: $C + \frac{1}{2}O_2 \rightarrow CO$; $\Delta H = -393.5 + 283.0 = -110.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: $-676.5$ adds the two values without reversing. $+110.5$ has the wrong sign. $-221.0$ is the value for forming 2 mol of CO.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting to change the sign when reversing the CO combustion equation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Hess's law of constant heat summation
questions.question: The standard enthalpies of combustion of $C(graphite)$, $H_2(g)$ and $CH_4(g)$ are $-393.5$, $-285.8$ and $-890.3$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ respectively, with water formed as $H_2O(l)$. What is the standard enthalpy of formation of $CH_4(g)$?

solution.key_concept: Hess's law: combine the combustion equations so that they add up to the formation reaction.
steps: Target reaction: $C + 2H_2 \rightarrow CH_4$.
$\Delta_f H = \Delta_c H(C) + 2\Delta_c H(H_2) - \Delta_c H(CH_4)$
solution.why_not_others: $+74.8$ has the wrong sign. $+211.0$ forgets to multiply the $H_2$ value by 2. $-1855.4$ adds all three values without reversing the $CH_4$ combustion.
solution.common_trap: Not multiplying the $H_2$ combustion enthalpy by its coefficient of 2.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Hess's law of constant heat summation
questions.question: Given: $S(s) + O_2(g) \rightarrow SO_2(g)$; $\Delta H = -297$ kJ and $S(s) + \frac{3}{2}O_2(g) \rightarrow SO_3(g)$; $\Delta H = -396$ kJ. What is $\Delta H$ for the reaction $SO_2(g) + \frac{1}{2}O_2(g) \rightarrow SO_3(g)$?

solution.key_concept: Reverse the first equation and add it to the second (Hess's law).
steps: Reverse the first equation: $SO_2 \rightarrow S + O_2$; $\Delta H = +297$ kJ.
Add the second equation: $SO_2 + \frac{1}{2}O_2 \rightarrow SO_3$.
solution.why_not_others: $-693$ adds the values without reversing. $+99$ has the wrong sign. $-198$ is the value for 2 mol of $SO_2$.
solution.common_trap: Adding the given $\Delta H$ values directly without reversing the $SO_2$ equation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Hess's law of constant heat summation
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: $\Delta H$ values of the two equations are summed

solution.key_concept: Thermochemical equations can be handled like algebraic equations, and Hess's law underlies the Born-Haber cycle.
steps: Reversing a reaction changes the sign of $\Delta H$: A-III.
Multiplying a reaction by a factor multiplies $\Delta H$ by that factor: B-IV.
Adding reactions adds their $\Delta H$ values: C-I.
The Born-Haber cycle gives lattice enthalpy: D-II.
solution.why_not_others: Each of the other options swaps at least one pair of operations and their effects.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that multiplying an equation changes the sign, or that reversing it changes the magnitude.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Hess's law of constant heat summation
questions.question: Which of the following statements about Hess's law are correct?

statements.A: Hess's law holds because enthalpy is a state function.
statements.B: Reversing a thermochemical equation leaves both the magnitude and the sign of $\Delta H$ unchanged.
statements.C: The physical states of all species must match when thermochemical equations are combined.
statements.D: Hess's law allows calculation of enthalpies that cannot be measured directly, such as the enthalpy of formation of CO.
statements.E: The total enthalpy change of a reaction depends on the number of intermediate steps through which it is carried out.

options: A, C, D and E only

solution.key_concept: Enthalpy is a state function, so $\Delta H$ depends only on the initial and final states.
steps: A is correct: it is the basis of Hess's law.
B is incorrect: reversing a reaction changes the sign of $\Delta H$.
C is correct: $H_2O(l)$ and $H_2O(g)$, for example, have different enthalpies.
D is correct: $\Delta_f H$ of CO is the classic example.
E is incorrect: $\Delta H$ does not depend on the path or the number of steps.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) includes the false B. Option (2) includes the false E. Option (3) includes both B and E.
solution.common_trap: Believing that more steps change the total $\Delta H$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Once B and E are identified as false, only option (4) is left.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpies of bond dissociation, combustion, formation, atomization, sublimation, phase transition, hydration, ionization and solution
questions.question: For which of the following is the standard enthalpy of formation NOT zero?

solution.key_concept: $\Delta_f H^\circ = 0$ only for the reference (most stable) form of an element.
steps: Graphite, $O_2(g)$ and $Br_2(l)$ are reference forms, so their $\Delta_f H^\circ = 0$.
Diamond is not the reference form of carbon, so its $\Delta_f H^\circ \neq 0$.
solution.why_not_others: The other three are elements in their standard reference states.
solution.common_trap: Treating every form of an element as having $\Delta_f H^\circ = 0$, or overlooking that bromine's reference state is a liquid.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpies of bond dissociation, combustion, formation, atomization, sublimation, phase transition, hydration, ionization and solution
questions.question: Using the bond enthalpies H-H = 436 kJ mol$^{-1}$, Cl-Cl = 242 kJ mol$^{-1}$ and H-Cl = 431 kJ mol$^{-1}$, calculate $\Delta_r H$ for the reaction as written: $H_2(g) + Cl_2(g) \rightarrow 2HCl(g)$.

solution.key_concept: $\Delta_r H = \sum BE(\text{reactants}) - \sum BE(\text{products})$
steps: Bonds broken: $436 + 242 = 678$ kJ.
Bonds formed: $2 \times 431 = 862$ kJ.
solution.why_not_others: $+184$ uses products minus reactants. $+247$ counts only one H-Cl bond. $-92$ is the value per mole of HCl, not for the reaction as written.
solution.common_trap: Applying the formation-enthalpy order (products minus reactants) to bond enthalpies.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpies of bond dissociation, combustion, formation, atomization, sublimation, phase transition, hydration, ionization and solution
questions.question: The enthalpy of atomization of $CH_4(g)$ is 1664 kJ mol$^{-1}$. What is the average C-H bond enthalpy?

solution.key_concept: For $CH_4$, $\Delta_a H$ = 4 × average C-H bond enthalpy.
steps: $CH_4(g) \rightarrow C(g) + 4H(g)$ breaks four C-H bonds.
Average C-H bond enthalpy = $1664 / 4 = 416$ kJ mol$^{-1}$
solution.why_not_others: 1664 is the total for all four bonds. 832 divides by 2, and 555 divides by 3.
solution.common_trap: Equating the atomization enthalpy with a single bond enthalpy, which is true only for diatomic molecules like $H_2$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpies of bond dissociation, combustion, formation, atomization, sublimation, phase transition, hydration, ionization and solution
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Dissolution of $NH_4Cl$ in water is endothermic.
statements.R: For $NH_4Cl$, the lattice enthalpy exceeds the magnitude of the hydration enthalpy.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: $\Delta_{sol}H = \Delta_{lattice}H + \Delta_{hyd}H$
steps: Lattice enthalpy is positive and hydration enthalpy is negative.
If the lattice enthalpy exceeds $|\Delta_{hyd}H|$, then $\Delta_{sol}H > 0$.
This is the case for $NH_4Cl$, so its dissolution is endothermic, and R explains A.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, and R gives exactly the reason for A.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that every dissolution is exothermic because hydration releases energy.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpies of bond dissociation, combustion, formation, atomization, sublimation, phase transition, hydration, ionization and solution
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Bond dissociation enthalpy, ionization enthalpy and hydration enthalpy are all positive quantities.
statements.II: For a given substance, the enthalpy of vaporization is greater than its enthalpy of sublimation.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: The sign of each enthalpy type, and the relation $\Delta_{sub}H = \Delta_{fus}H + \Delta_{vap}H$.
steps: Hydration enthalpy is negative, so Statement I is false.
$\Delta_{sub}H = \Delta_{fus}H + \Delta_{vap}H$, so $\Delta_{sub}H > \Delta_{vap}H$.
Statement II states the reverse, so it is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I wrongly calls hydration enthalpy positive. Statement II reverses the correct inequality.
solution.common_trap: Grouping hydration enthalpy with the endothermic quantities.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Second law of thermodynamics and spontaneity
questions.question: In which of the following processes does the entropy of the system decrease?
options: Dissolution of a salt in water

solution.key_concept: Entropy order: $S_{gas} \gg S_{liquid} > S_{solid}$. Entropy increases on melting, vaporization and dissolution.
steps: Freezing converts a liquid into a more ordered solid.
So $\Delta S < 0$ for freezing.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Freezing of water to ice
solution.why_not_others: Melting, evaporation and dissolution all increase disorder, so $\Delta S > 0$ for each.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that dissolution decreases entropy.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Second law of thermodynamics and spontaneity
questions.question: The enthalpy of fusion of ice is 6.0 kJ mol$^{-1}$ at its melting point of 273 K. What is the molar entropy of fusion of ice?

solution.key_concept: $\Delta S_{trans} = \frac{\Delta H_{trans}}{T_{trans}}$
steps: Convert to joules: $\Delta_{fus}H = 6000$ J mol$^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: 0.022 comes from keeping kJ but quoting the result in J. 1638 multiplies by T instead of dividing. $-22.0$ has the wrong sign, since melting increases entropy.
solution.common_trap: Not converting kJ to J before dividing.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Second law of thermodynamics and spontaneity
questions.question: 1 mol of an ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly at 300 K from 2 L to 20 L. What is the entropy change of the gas? (R = 8.314 J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)

solution.key_concept: $\Delta S = 2.303\,nR\log\frac{V_2}{V_1}$ for isothermal expansion of an ideal gas.
steps: $\Delta S = 2.303 \times 1 \times 8.314 \times 1$
$\Delta S \approx 19.15$ J K$^{-1}$
solution.why_not_others: 0 would apply to a reversible adiabatic process, not an isothermal one. 8.314 leaves out the factor 2.303. The negative value would mean a compression.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that an isothermal process has zero entropy change because T is constant.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Second law of thermodynamics and spontaneity
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Free expansion of an ideal gas

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Vaporization of a liquid at its boiling point

solution.key_concept: Entropy changes for special processes and the second law.
steps: Free expansion: $\Delta S_{sys} = nR\ln(V_2/V_1)$ and $\Delta S_{surr} = 0$: A-III.
Reversible adiabatic process: $q_{rev} = 0$, so $\Delta S = 0$: B-I.
Phase transition at its transition temperature: $\Delta S = \Delta H/T$: C-IV.
Second law: $\Delta S_{universe} > 0$ for a spontaneous process: D-II.
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) gives free expansion $\Delta S = 0$. Options (3) and (4) misplace the second-law and transition entries.
solution.common_trap: Taking $\Delta S_{sys} = 0$ for free expansion because q = 0.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Second law of thermodynamics and spontaneity
questions.question: Which of the following statements about entropy and spontaneity are correct?

statements.B: Melting of ice above 273 K is spontaneous even though it is endothermic.
statements.C: At equilibrium, the entropy of the universe remains constant.
statements.D: A given quantity of heat causes a greater entropy increase at a higher temperature than at a lower temperature.

solution.key_concept: Second law: $\Delta S_{universe} > 0$ for a spontaneous process and $= 0$ at equilibrium. Also $\Delta S = q_{rev}/T$.
steps: A is false: exothermic character alone does not decide spontaneity.
B is true: this is the standard example of a spontaneous endothermic process.
C is true: this is a statement of the second law.
D is false: since $\Delta S = q/T$, the same q gives a larger $\Delta S$ at lower T.
E is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): B, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Options (1), (3) and (4) each include the false statement A or D.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that a higher temperature gives a larger entropy change for the same heat.
solution.time_saving_tip: Rejecting A and D leaves only option (2).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Entropy of the universe and Gibbs energy as criteria for spontaneity
questions.question: A reaction has $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$. Assuming $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ do not change with temperature, under which condition is the reaction spontaneous at constant pressure?
options: Only at high temperatures, above $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$
Only at low temperatures, below $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$

solution.key_concept: Spontaneity at constant T and p is decided by the sign of $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$.
steps: Here $\Delta H > 0$ works against spontaneity, while $-T\Delta S < 0$ works for it.
The $T\Delta S$ term becomes larger than $\Delta H$ only when T is high enough.
So $\Delta G < 0$ only when $T > \Delta H/\Delta S$.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Only at high temperatures, above $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$
solution.why_not_others: Spontaneity at all temperatures needs $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$. Spontaneity at no temperature needs $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S < 0$. Spontaneity only at low temperatures needs both $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ to be negative.
solution.common_trap: Assuming an endothermic reaction can never be spontaneous.
solution.time_saving_tip: When $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ have the same sign, the sign of $\Delta S$ tells you whether the reaction is favoured at high or low temperature.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Entropy of the universe and Gibbs energy as criteria for spontaneity
questions.question: For a reaction, $\Delta H = +180\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ and $\Delta S = +150\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$. Assuming both values are independent of temperature, the reaction is spontaneous:

solution.key_concept: Crossover temperature $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$, with both quantities in the same energy unit.
steps: Convert $\Delta H$ to joules: $\Delta H = 180000\ J\ mol^{-1}$.
Calculate the crossover temperature: $T = 180000/150 = 1200\ K$.
Both $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are positive, so $\Delta G < 0$ only above 1200 K.
solution.why_not_others: 1.2 K comes from leaving $\Delta H$ in kJ while $\Delta S$ is in J. 927 K wrongly subtracts 273 from a temperature that is already in kelvin. 'Below 1200 K' reverses the direction that applies when $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are both positive.
solution.common_trap: Mixing kJ and J when calculating $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Entropy of the universe and Gibbs energy as criteria for spontaneity
questions.question: For a process at 250 K and constant pressure, $\Delta H_{sys} = -50\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ and $\Delta S_{sys} = -150\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$. The total entropy change of the universe and the Gibbs energy change of the process are, respectively:

solution.key_concept: $\Delta S_{surr} = -\Delta H_{sys}/T$ and $\Delta G = -T\Delta S_{total}$.
steps: Add the system term: $\Delta S_{total} = -150 + 200 = +50\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$.
Then $\Delta G = -T\Delta S_{total} = -250 \times 50 = -12500\ J\ mol^{-1} = -12.5\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) takes $\Delta S_{surr}$ with the wrong sign. Option (2) treats $\Delta S_{sys}$ as positive. Option (3) drops the minus sign in $\Delta G = -T\Delta S_{total}$.
solution.common_trap: Writing $\Delta S_{surr} = +\Delta H_{sys}/T$ instead of $-\Delta H_{sys}/T$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Once you have $\Delta S_{total} > 0$, $\Delta G$ must be negative, which eliminates options (1) and (3) straight away.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Entropy of the universe and Gibbs energy as criteria for spontaneity
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A reaction with $\Delta G < 0$ at constant temperature and pressure may still proceed at an extremely slow rate.
statements.R: The decrease in Gibbs energy, $-\Delta G$, equals the maximum useful (non-pV) work that can be obtained from a process.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Spontaneity criteria say nothing about rate, and $-\Delta G$ is the maximum non-expansion work.
steps: A is true because $\Delta G < 0$ only shows that a reaction is spontaneous; it says nothing about its rate.
R is true because $-\Delta G = w_{useful,max}$.
R describes the work interpretation of $\Delta G$. It does not explain why a spontaneous reaction can be slow.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: R is not the reason for A; the correct explanation is that thermodynamics does not predict rate. Both statements are true, so options (3) and (4) are wrong.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that a negative $\Delta G$ means a fast reaction.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Entropy of the universe and Gibbs energy as criteria for spontaneity
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: At constant temperature and pressure, $\Delta G = -T\Delta S_{total}$, so a positive entropy change of the universe necessarily corresponds to a negative Gibbs energy change of the system.
statements.II: For a reaction with $\Delta H = -120\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ and $\Delta S = -300\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$ (both independent of temperature), $\Delta G$ is negative at 300 K but positive at 500 K.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: $\Delta G = -T\Delta S_{total}$; when $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are both negative, the reaction is spontaneous only below $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$.
steps: Statement I: T is always positive, so $\Delta S_{total} > 0$ gives $\Delta G < 0$. Statement I is correct.
Statement II, crossover temperature: $T = 120000/300 = 400\ K$.
At 300 K: $\Delta G = -120 + 300(0.300) = -30\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$, which is negative.
At 500 K: $\Delta G = -120 + 500(0.300) = +30\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$, which is positive. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements check out by calculation, so every option that marks either statement incorrect is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Assuming an exothermic reaction is spontaneous at every temperature.
solution.time_saving_tip: Find the crossover temperature (400 K) first. If both $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are negative, the reaction is spontaneous below it and non-spontaneous above it.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Standard Gibbs energy change and equilibrium constant
questions.question: For a reaction at 298 K, the standard Gibbs energy change $\Delta_r G^\circ$ is positive. Which of the following is correct about its equilibrium constant K?

solution.key_concept: $\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT\ln K$
steps: If $\Delta_r G^\circ > 0$, then $\ln K < 0$.
This means $0 < K < 1$, so the equilibrium mixture favours reactants.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): K < 1 and reactants are favoured
solution.why_not_others: K > 1 requires a negative $\Delta_r G^\circ$. K = 1 requires $\Delta_r G^\circ = 0$. K is an exponential, $K = e^{-\Delta_r G^\circ/RT}$, so it can never be negative.
solution.common_trap: Confusing a negative $\ln K$ with a negative K.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Standard Gibbs energy change and equilibrium constant
questions.question: The equilibrium constant of a reaction at 298 K is $1.0 \times 10^{3}$. What is the standard Gibbs energy change of the reaction? ($R = 8.314\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$)

solution.key_concept: $\Delta_r G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$
steps: Calculate $2.303RT = 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298 \approx 5706\ J\ mol^{-1}$.
Here $\log K = 3$.
So $\Delta_r G^\circ = -5706 \times 3 = -17117\ J\ mol^{-1} \approx -17.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: $+17.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ has the wrong sign, since K > 1 requires a negative $\Delta_r G^\circ$. $-7.43\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ leaves out the factor 2.303. $-17117\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ labels a value in joules as kJ.
solution.common_trap: Using $\log K$ with $RT$ instead of $2.303RT$, or mixing up J and kJ.
solution.time_saving_tip: At 298 K, $\Delta G^\circ$ changes by about 5.7 kJ for every factor of 10 in K, so $\Delta G^\circ \approx -3 \times 5.7 = -17.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Standard Gibbs energy change and equilibrium constant
questions.question: For a gas-phase reaction at 298 K, $\Delta H^\circ = +3.5\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = +50\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$. Taking $2.303RT = 5.7\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ at 298 K, the equilibrium constant of the reaction is approximately:

solution.key_concept: $-2.303RT\log K = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$
steps: Calculate $T\Delta S^\circ = 298 \times 0.050 = 14.9\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.
Then $\Delta G^\circ = 3.5 - 14.9 = -11.4\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.
Therefore $K = 10^2 = 100$.
solution.why_not_others: 0.01 comes from a sign error in $\Delta G^\circ$. 4.6 is the value of $\ln K$, not K. 2 is the value of $\log K$, not K.
solution.common_trap: Stopping at $\log K$ or $\ln K$ and reporting it as K.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Standard Gibbs energy change and equilibrium constant
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Tenfold increase in K at 298 K

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: $\Delta_r G^\circ$ lowered by about $5.7\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$

solution.key_concept: $\Delta_r G = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ and $\Delta_r G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$
steps: A: a negative $\Delta_r G^\circ$ gives K > 1, so A matches III.
B: $\Delta_r G^\circ = 0$ gives K = 1, so B matches I.
C: at equilibrium $\Delta_r G = 0$ and Q = K, so C matches IV.
D: since $2.303RT \approx 5.7\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$, each tenfold increase in K lowers $\Delta_r G^\circ$ by about 5.7 kJ, so D matches II.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps K = 1 and K > 1. Option (2) wrongly treats every equilibrium as having K = 1, i.e. $\Delta_r G^\circ = 0$. Option (4) assigns the 5.7 kJ shift to A.
solution.common_trap: Believing that $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ at every equilibrium.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Standard Gibbs energy change and equilibrium constant
questions.question: Which of the following statements about Gibbs energy and the equilibrium constant are correct?

statements.A: At equilibrium $\Delta_r G = 0$, but $\Delta_r G^\circ$ is generally not zero.
statements.B: If equal concentrations of N and D exist at equilibrium in $N \rightleftharpoons D$ at temperature T, then $\Delta S^\circ = \Delta H^\circ/T$.
statements.C: Since $\Delta_r G = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$, $\Delta_r G$ is negative whenever Q < K.
statements.D: A reaction with $K = 10^{-3}$ at 298 K has $\Delta_r G^\circ \approx -17.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.

solution.key_concept: $\Delta_r G = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$, which can be written as $RT\ln(Q/K)$.
steps: A is correct: $\Delta G^\circ$ is zero only when K = 1.
B is correct: equal concentrations give K = 1, so $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ and $\Delta H^\circ = T\Delta S^\circ$.
C is correct: substituting $\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ gives $\Delta_r G = RT\ln(Q/K)$, which is negative when Q < K.
D is incorrect: $\Delta_r G^\circ = -5.7 \times (-3) = +17.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and C only
solution.why_not_others: D has the wrong sign, which rules out options (3) and (4). Option (2) leaves out C, which is correct.
solution.common_trap: Getting the sign of $\Delta G^\circ$ wrong when K < 1.
solution.time_saving_tip: K < 1 always means a positive $\Delta G^\circ$, so D can be rejected without any calculation.
